headline: Broad law authorizes Army Corps of Engineers water projects and studies, renews economic development programs, shifts highway funds, and sets federal office-use rules.
what_it_does: The law lets the Army Corps of Engineers start or speed up hundreds of flood control, harbor, dredging, ecosystem, and water supply projects and studies, and cancels some old unbuilt ones. It changes cost-sharing rules, often lowering the local share to 10% for projects that help economically disadvantaged communities. It also renews Economic Development Administration grant programs and regional commissions through 2029, creates two new regional commissions, and moves unused highway loan money (TIFIA) to states. It requires federal agencies to measure how much they use their office buildings and aim for at least 60% use, and orders the sale of some federal buildings.

who_it_affects.group: States, local governments, and tribes that partner with the Army Corps
who_it_affects.how: They get more guidance, new advisors, and in some cases a smaller share of project costs, and tribes may carry out some projects directly.

who_it_affects.group: Residents of flood-prone and coastal communities
who_it_affects.how: New and expanded flood, storm, levee, and dam safety projects and studies are authorized in many named locations.

who_it_affects.group: Ports, barge operators, and shipping businesses
who_it_affects.how: The federal government pays a larger share of costs for certain deeper harbors and inland waterway projects.
They gain wider access to Economic Development Administration grants, including for broadband, workforce training, and areas hurt by coal or industry job losses.
They receive $1.8 billion plus later portions of unused TIFIA highway loan funds to spend on federal-aid highway projects.

who_it_affects.group: People in Delaware, Maryland, Pennsylvania, Rhode Island, Massachusetts, and Connecticut
who_it_affects.how: New regional commissions are created to fund economic development in their counties.
Agencies must track office occupancy and may have space cut or consolidated if buildings are used less than 60% on average.
The Corps may keep recreation fees if most are spent on the site, and must post updated site status and access information.
The Denali Commission is renewed and a new housing fund supports low- and moderate-income housing and housing for public workers.

when_it_takes_effect: Enacted January 4, 2025; many provisions have their own deadlines, such as highway fund transfers on April 1, 2025 and April 1, 2026, and program authorizations running through FY2028–FY2030.
